content: The revised recommendations from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) address the prevention of plague and update prior guidelines. Plague is an acute, often fatal, and potentially epidemic disease caused by Yersinia pestis. This bacterium is maintained in natural enzootic cycles involving wild rodents and their fleas in specific regions of Asia, Africa, the Americas, and southeastern Europe near the Caspian Sea. These cycles may remain unnoticed without human transmission or may lead to sporadic human cases. Epidemics can occur when the disease spreads from wild rodents to rat populations (Rattus genus) living near human habitats. Due to its high fatality rate and epidemic potential, plague is classified as a Class I notifiable disease under International Health Regulations, requiring all suspected cases to be reported to public health authorities and confirmed cases to be reported to the World Health Organization (WHO). In the United States, suspected plague cases must be reported to state health departments, which notify the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Laboratory-confirmed cases are subsequently reported by the CDC to the WHO. Characteristics of Plague Etiologic Agent Yersinia pestis is a gram-negative coccobacillus belonging to the Enterobacteriaceae family. Its virulence and survival in mammalian hosts and flea vectors depend on several chromosomal and plasmid-associated factors. Modes of Transmission and Disease Description The most common mode of transmission to humans is through the bite of infected fleas. Other routes include direct contact with infected animals or inhalation of infectious respiratory droplets. Infection results in a severe febrile illness characterized by headache, myalgia, malaise, shaking chills, prostration, and gastrointestinal symptoms. The three main clinical forms of plague are bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic. Bubonic plague is the most common form, accounting for 80–90% of U.S. cases. It is characterized by acute regional lymphadenopathy (buboes), typically involving lymph nodes draining the site of initial infection, such as the inguinal, axillary, or cervical regions. The incubation period is 2–6 days, and untreated cases have a fatality rate of 50–60%. Septicemic plague occurs when Y. pestis spreads to the bloodstream, either as a primary condition or secondary to bubonic plague. Complications include septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, meningitis, and coma. During 1947–1977 in the U.S., approximately 10% of plague patients presented with septicemic plague, with a 50% fatality rate. Pneumonic plague is the least common but most dangerous form. It can develop as a secondary complication of septicemic plague or from inhaling infectious respiratory droplets. Symptoms include severe pneumonia, high fever, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. The incubation period is 1–3 days, and untreated patients rarely survive beyond 18 hours after the onset of respiratory symptoms. Ecology Y. pestis is maintained in enzootic and epizootic cycles involving susceptible wild rodents and their fleas. Human risk is highest during epizootics, which cause high mortality in commensal rat populations, forcing infected fleas to seek alternative hosts, including humans. Carnivores and rabbits may occasionally become infected but are incidental hosts. Carnivores, however, may contribute to the geographic spread of infected fleas. Epidemiology Between 1980 and 1994, 18,739 human plague cases were reported to the WHO from 20 countries, with an average of 1,087 cases per year. Plague is underreported in many countries with inadequate surveillance and laboratory capabilities. Epidemics are more likely in areas with poor sanitation and large rat populations. In the U.S., 341 human cases were reported to the CDC between 1970 and 1995, with 80% occurring in the southwestern states of New Mexico, Arizona, and Colorado. Most cases are acquired near the patient’s residence during summer months when exposure to infected fleas is greatest. Plague Vaccine History Killed bacterial vaccines have been used since 1896. Currently, only one vaccine—a formalin-inactivated preparation—is licensed for use in the U.S. This vaccine is manufactured by Greer Laboratories, Inc. Live attenuated Y. pestis vaccines have been developed but are not commercially available, and their safety and efficacy remain untested. Immunogenicity and Efficacy The efficacy of the inactivated vaccine in humans has not been measured in controlled studies. Indirect evidence from U.S. military personnel in Vietnam suggests the vaccine may prevent flea-borne plague. However, it is unclear whether vaccination protects against infectious respiratory droplets or aerosols. At least two vaccinated individuals have developed pneumonic plague, indicating limited efficacy in preventing inhalation-based infections. Laboratory studies in animals suggest that antibodies to the Fraction 1 (F1) capsular antigen of Y. pestis are strongly protective. Vaccine Administration Vaccination is recommended only for individuals at high risk of exposure, such as laboratory personnel handling viable Y. pestis and field workers in plague-endemic areas. Vaccinated individuals should still follow preventive measures due to uncertainties about vaccine efficacy. Vaccination is not intended for controlling plague epidemics, as it requires months to complete the primary series and develop protective antibody levels. Adverse Reactions Adverse reactions are generally mild but may increase in frequency and severity with repeated doses. Common reactions include local erythema, induration, malaise, headache, fever, and lymphadenopathy. Severe reactions, such as anaphylaxis, are rare. Adverse events should be reported to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). Precautions and Contraindications Vaccination is contraindicated in individuals with a history of hypersensitivity to the vaccine or its components. Pregnant women should be vaccinated only if the potential benefits outweigh the risks to the fetus. Immunocompromised individuals may not develop protective antibody levels and should have their antibody titers monitored when possible. Preventive Measures Plague prevention relies on personal protective measures, insecticide applications, avoidance of sick or dead animals, and environmental modifications to reduce rodent populations. Prophylactic antibiotic therapy is recommended for individuals presumed to have been exposed to infection. Vaccination is generally unnecessary when appropriate preventive measures are taken. Conclusion Plague is an acute bacterial illness typically transmitted to humans through flea bites, direct contact with infected animals, or inhalation of infectious respiratory droplets. While the inactivated plague vaccine has been available since World War II, its efficacy in protecting humans remains inadequately demonstrated. Pneumonic plague has developed in vaccinated individuals, indicating limited protection against inhalation-based infections. However, the vaccine appears effective in preventing flea-borne transmission. Vaccination is recommended for laboratory personnel and individuals with regular contact with wild-rodent hosts in plague-endemic areas.
